title: Aircraft Systems — Engine, Fuel, Electrical, Pitot-Static, and Gyroscopic Instruments

questions.text: During cruise at 7,500 feet on a humid day with OAT of 55°F, the RPM begins dropping gradually and the engine runs slightly rough. Carburetor heat has not been applied. What is the MOST likely cause and correct immediate action?

options.label: A
options.text: Fuel starvation — the fuel selector should be switched to the fullest tank immediately; a gradual RPM drop indicates insufficient fuel flow to the carburetor rather than carburetor ice, which would cause abrupt power loss rather than gradual reduction

options.label: B
options.text: Carburetor ice — conditions of 55°F OAT and high humidity are in the prime carburetor ice formation zone (20°F to 70°F OAT with humidity); the immediate action is to apply CARBURETOR HEAT FULL ON; expect initial roughness as the ice melts and water passes through the engine, followed by smooth power restoration

options.label: C
options.text: Magneto failure — a gradual RPM drop with rough running is the classic symptom of single magneto failure; the correct immediate action is to perform a magneto check by cycling the ignition switch from BOTH to LEFT to RIGHT; if one magneto shows significant RPM drop, land at the nearest airport

options.label: D
options.text: Lean mixture — at 7,500 feet on a warm day, the mixture may have auto-richened due to changing OAT and altitude combination; adjust the mixture control to the lean side until RPM recovers; carburetor ice is only a concern below 3,500 feet AGL where humidity is higher

questions.explanation: Carburetor ice is the most likely diagnosis at 55°F OAT with high humidity. The carburetor ice prime zone is approximately 20°F to 70°F OAT with relative humidity above 40-50% — pilots frequently underestimate this because 55°F does not feel like 'icing' conditions. In a carbureted engine, the venturi effect and fuel vaporization drop the carburetor throat temperature 20-30°C below ambient — easily into ice formation territory at 55°F OAT. Gradual RPM drop (with fixed-pitch prop) and rough running are the textbook carburetor ice symptoms. Immediate action: FULL carburetor heat ON. The initial response will likely be rougher running and momentary RPM drop as water from melting ice passes through — this is expected and confirms the diagnosis. Once ice clears, RPM returns to normal and running smooths. If heat is delayed, ice can fully block the venturi causing complete engine stoppage. Options A, C, and D describe alternative diagnoses with legitimate symptoms but are not supported by the environmental fingerprint (55°F + humidity) that points directly to carb ice.

questions.text: During preflight sump drain inspection, the pilot takes a fuel sample and notes: the fuel in the cup is straw-yellow/clear colored rather than blue. The ramp agent says 'we topped it off this morning with what came out of the main fuel truck.' What is the most critical concern and correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Minor concern only — avgas 100LL occasionally appears clear or yellow due to age; the blue dye fades over time in storage; the pilot should smell the fuel to confirm it is avgas and proceed if the smell matches the stored fuel used on previous flights

options.label: B
options.text: Suspected fuel contamination or misfueling — Jet-A aviation fuel is straw/clear colored; avgas 100LL is distinctly blue; clear or straw-colored fuel in a piston aircraft tank is a critical indication of possible Jet-A misfueling; the pilot must not fly, must contact the FBO immediately, must test the fuel with an avgas water detector or lab test, and must have the aircraft inspected before any flight

options.label: C
options.text: Water contamination — clear fuel appearing beneath the blue avgas indicates water has displaced the dye at the bottom of the tank; drain more samples until the blue color returns; if blue color returns consistently, the water has been flushed and the flight may proceed

options.label: D
options.text: The blue dye in 100LL is only visible in bulk quantities; in small sump drain samples (2-4 oz), 100LL commonly appears clear or pale yellow because the blue dye concentration is too low to be visible in small volumes; this is normal and does not indicate misfueling

questions.explanation: The color identification of aviation fuel is a hard safety standard: 100LL Avgas: BLUE (Prussian blue dye added specifically for visual identification). Jet-A: CLEAR to STRAW/LIGHT YELLOW. A piston aircraft that has been misfueled with Jet-A may cause immediate and catastrophic engine failure on takeoff or shortly after departure. Jet-A cannot be used in piston engines — the octane rating (approximately 45) is far below the 100 octane minimum for piston compression ratios. The consequence: detonation failure, which can destroy the engine in seconds. Straw/clear fuel in a piston aircraft must be treated as a misfueling emergency: do not start or taxi, do not fly, drain all fuel from the sumps and tanks, contact the FBO, have the fuel tested. Option A is wrong — 100LL blue dye is a stable additive that does not fade. Option C incorrectly attributes a clear layer beneath blue to water — water would appear as a clear or slightly cloudy layer below blue fuel, but a completely straw-colored sample is not water. Option D is completely false — 100LL is distinctly blue even in small sump samples; a clear sump sample from a 100LL-topped tank is a serious anomaly.

questions.text: In IMC on an IFR flight, the pilot notices: the altimeter is frozen at 8,500 feet, the VSI reads zero, and the airspeed appears to be increasing as the aircraft descends. What has occurred and what is the correct procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: A vacuum pump failure has occurred — the altimeter and VSI are gyroscopic instruments and have lost their gyro power source; the correct action is to switch to the backup electric gyro and use the electric attitude indicator for pitch reference

options.label: B
options.text: The static port is blocked — the static system instruments (altimeter and VSI) are frozen because they cannot sense changing static pressure; the airspeed appearing to increase during descent is the characteristic static blockage ASI error (actual ram air pressure increases against frozen static reference, falsely showing speed increase); the correct action is to select the ALTERNATE STATIC SOURCE to restore accurate static pressure readings

options.label: C
options.text: The pitot tube is blocked — a blocked pitot causes all three instruments (ASI, ALT, VSI) to fail simultaneously; the pilot should use the magnetic compass for heading and the engine gauges for power management; declare an emergency on 121.5

options.label: D
options.text: The aircraft has exceeded its maximum airspeed — the VSI and altimeter have protection modes that freeze their readings above Vne; the airspeed increase confirms the overspeed condition; the pilot should immediately reduce power and extend speed brakes to recover below Vne

questions.explanation: This question tests knowledge of the specific, distinctive pattern of a blocked static port: (1) ALTIMETER: freezes at the altitude where blockage occurred — cannot sense the pressure change needed to display different altitude. (2) VSI: freezes at zero — cannot detect the differential pressure change (rate of change of static pressure) that drives the VSI. (3) ASI: shows false readings — the static port blockage traps a lower static pressure reference; as the aircraft descends into higher-pressure air, the DIFFERENTIAL between pitot (increasing) and the trapped static pressure increases, making the ASI appear to INCREASE even as the aircraft descends. This is the key diagnostic: if ASI increases during a verified descent, the static port is blocked. Correct action: alternate static source. Option A incorrectly identifies these as vacuum-powered instruments — the altimeter, VSI, and ASI are pitot-static instruments, not gyroscopic. A vacuum pump failure affects the Attitude Indicator and Heading Indicator. Option C incorrectly attributes all three failures to a blocked pitot — a blocked pitot only affects the ASI (directly); the ALT and VSI are static-only instruments unaffected by pitot blockage.

questions.text: While climbing through 5,000 feet, the pilot notices the attitude indicator is slowly tilting to the right even though the aircraft appears to be wings-level based on outside visual reference. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Magnetic variation — the attitude indicator is referenced to magnetic north like the compass; when crossing through large magnetic declination zones, the AI slowly rotates to display the declination change; this is normal in mountainous areas with large magnetic anomalies

options.label: B
options.text: Gyroscopic precession — a prolonged climbing turn (even a coordinated one) applies a precessive force to the AI gyroscope 90° ahead of the applied force direction; this causes the AI to slowly tilt from the true wings-level attitude; the AI erecting mechanism continuously corrects this but during prolonged maneuvers the display temporarily diverges from actual attitude

options.label: C
options.text: Vacuum pump failure — when the vacuum pump fails, the AI gyroscope gradually spins down; as it decelerates, rigidity decreases and the gyroscope becomes susceptible to Earth's rotation; the resulting drift causes the AI to tilt slowly during climb phases; this is the initial symptom of impending AI failure

options.label: D
options.text: Normal AI drift — attitude indicators drift 3 to 5 degrees per minute as a design characteristic; a 10-minute climb from pattern altitude to 5,000 feet accumulates 30-50 degrees of drift; pilots should expect this and cross-check frequently

questions.explanation: The AI uses gyroscopic rigidity to maintain a stable attitude reference. However, gyroscopes are subject to precession: when a force is applied to a spinning gyro, it reacts 90° in the direction of rotation from the point of force application. During prolonged turns, the erecting mechanism can be overpowered by precessional forces, causing the AI display to slowly drift from the true attitude. This is most noticeable in prolonged climbing turns, descending turns, or sustained coordinated maneuvers. The ai has an erecting mechanism that continuously works to align the gyro with the vertical (gravity sensing), but this process is not instantaneous — there can be lag during dynamic maneuvers. In this scenario (climbing), even a slight bank held for an extended period or any continued turning causes precessional drift. Cross-checking with outside visual reference and the turn coordinator (electrically powered, not affected by vacuum or gyro precession in the same way) is correct procedure. Option C describes vacuum pump failure — which causes the AI to slowly tumble (not gradually drift), and is typically more abrupt once the gyro spools down. Option D dramatically overstates normal AI drift rate — 3-5°/minute drift is typical of the compass, not the AI.

questions.text: During an IFR flight in IMC, the vacuum pump fails. Which instruments remain reliable and which require immediate cross-check verification?

options.label: A
options.text: All instruments lose reliability — vacuum pump failure cascades to all instruments through the electrical bus; the pitot-static instruments experience dampened pressure sensing when the vacuum system fails because both share a common pressure manifold in most aircraft

options.label: B
options.text: VACUUM FAILURE AFFECTS: Attitude Indicator and Heading Indicator — these are gyro-driven by the vacuum pump and will begin to lose their gyroscopic rigidity (initially slowly, then increasingly erratic). REMAINS RELIABLE: Turn Coordinator (electric), Altimeter (static — no vacuum dependency), Airspeed Indicator (pitot-static — no vacuum dependency), VSI (static — no vacuum dependency), Magnetic Compass. Partial panel procedure: use Turn Coordinator + Altimeter + ASI + VSI + Clock for navigation and attitude control

options.label: C
options.text: VACUUM FAILURE AFFECTS: Turn Coordinator only — the turn coordinator is the only gyroscopic instrument powered by the vacuum system; the AI, HI, ALT, ASI, and VSI remain fully functional; the loss of the turn coordinator requires the pilot to use the AI as the primary bank reference

options.label: D
options.text: VACUUM FAILURE AFFECTS: Attitude Indicator, Heading Indicator, Altimeter, and VSI — all four share the vacuum manifold as their common power source in most certified light aircraft; the ASI and Turn Coordinator remain functional; declare an emergency and request radar vectors immediately

questions.explanation: Vacuum system failure is one of the most important instrument failure scenarios for IFR pilots. The power source for gyroscopic instruments in most light aircraft follows a specific division: Vacuum-powered: Attitude Indicator (AI) and Heading Indicator (HI / Direction Gyro). These will slowly fail as gyro spin rate decreases. Electrically powered: Turn Coordinator. This is intentionally on a different power source to provide redundancy. Pitot-static instruments (Altimeter, ASI, VSI): receive no power from either vacuum or electrical systems — they operate purely on air pressure differential and remain functional regardless of vacuum or electrical failure. Magnetic Compass: direct magnetic sensing, no dependency on either system. Partial panel procedure after vacuum failure: use Turn Coordinator for bank/rate information, Altimeter for altitude, ASI for airspeed, VSI for rate of altitude change, and a clock for timing turns. Option C reverses the power sources — the Turn Coordinator is electrically powered (survives vacuum failure), not vacuum-powered. The AI and HI are vacuum-powered (fail in vacuum failure). Option D incorrectly includes the Altimeter and VSI as vacuum-dependent — they are purely pitot-static instruments with no power dependency.

questions.text: During preflight fuel sump check, the pilot drains three clear samples from the left tank sump — each shows a small amount of water (clear bubbles below the blue fuel layer). The pilot drains twice more and still sees water. Under 14 CFR 91.7, may the pilot depart?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — if the pilot drains until the sample shows at least 90% blue fuel with only trace water bubbles, the water contamination is below the FAA threshold for fuel airworthiness; small residual amounts of water are permissible and are within the POH fuel system tolerance

options.label: B
options.text: No — persistent water in fuel samples indicates an ongoing source of water contamination (condensation, improper storage, rain incursion) that has not been resolved by sump draining; 14 CFR 91.7(a) prohibits operating an aircraft known to be in an unairworthy condition; water-contaminated fuel is an unairworthy condition; the flight must be grounded until the source of water is identified and the fuel system is cleared by a certificated mechanic

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — water in avgas is an anticipated condition addressed in the aircraft POH; the sump test instruction in most POH documents states 'drain until blue' as the standard; any sample showing predominant blue color with trace water is within the airworthiness standard and the flight may proceed

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — the fuel filter (gascolator) in the fuel system removes water before it reaches the carburetor; persistent water in the tank sump is a known storage artifact and does not represent a fuel system airworthiness concern; drain a final sample from the gascolator to confirm water removal

questions.explanation: 14 CFR 91.7(a) prohibits operating 'a civil aircraft that is not in an airworthy condition.' Persistent water in fuel after multiple sump drains is an airworthiness-compromising condition for two reasons: (1) Continued water presence indicates an unresolved source — condensation from overnight temperature differential, rain/moisture incursion through a fuel cap, or contaminated fuel supply. Draining will not resolve the source. (2) Any water entering the carburetor or fuel injection system can cause engine flameout. Even small water amounts at a critical moment (low-power descent, lean restart) can cause engine stoppage. The correct procedure when water persists: ground the aircraft, contact an A&P mechanic to identify the contamination source (inspect fuel caps for sealing, fuel sumps for structural cracks, fuel supply delivery records), drain and replace fuel if needed. Filing a report with the FBO about the fuel delivery is also appropriate. Option A and C invent FAA thresholds for 'permissible water levels' that do not exist — any water present in fuel is a concern; persistent water is a grounding condition. Option D incorrectly claims the gascolator removes all water — while the gascolator (main fuel strainer) has a sediment bowl and helps catch debris, it is not a complete water separator.

questions.text: During a VFR flight at 8,500 feet in visible moisture (light rain), the pilot notices gradual power loss and rough engine operation. Carburetor heat has not been applied because 'it's raining, not icing conditions.' The OAT is 48°F. The pilot applies carb heat. Engine roughness increases and RPM drops further momentarily. The pilot immediately pulls carb heat OFF, thinking 'the heat made it worse.' What error has occurred?

options.label: A
options.text: No error — pulling carb heat OFF is the correct response to increased roughness; carb heat causing roughness indicates the carburetor air intake is clean; the rough running has a different cause (magneto failure or spark plug fouling) that should be investigated separately

options.label: B
options.text: Critical error — the initial roughness and RPM drop after carb heat application is a NORMAL and EXPECTED response as melting ice (water) passes through the engine; this is the confirmation that carburetor ice was causing the original power loss; pulling carb heat OFF at this moment re-exposes the carburetor to icing conditions and allows ice to reform; carb heat should be maintained FULL ON until the engine smooths and RPM recovers

options.label: C
options.text: Partial error only — carb heat should have been applied earlier; however, once applied, the correct technique is to cycle carb heat ON for 10 seconds, then OFF for 10 seconds, in a pulse cycle; this prevents the ice from re-forming while not over-heating the carburetor which can cause vapor lock in warm avgas

options.label: D
options.text: No error — rain and visible moisture produce enough carburetor heating through water evaporation to prevent ice formation; the symptoms (rough running, RPM drop) confirm the engine needs an ignition check rather than carb heat; carb heat is designed for cold, dry, humid air scenarios not rainy conditions

questions.explanation: This scenario identifies the single most common carb heat management error: misinterpreting the expected initial roughness from carb heat as a sign that 'it wasn't carb ice.' Here is the complete carb heat response: (1) Carb ice present: ice partially blocks the venturi → reduced power, rough running. (2) Carb heat applied: hot air melts ice → water from ice passes through the carburetor and into the engine → this water causes momentary roughness and rpm drop — it may sound and feel WORSE initially. (3) If carb heat is maintained: ice fully melts, water clears, carburetor throat reopens → engine smooths, RPM recovers to normal. (4) If carb heat is removed prematurely (as in this scenario): the still-warm carburetor throat is immediately re-exposed to humid, near-freezing air → ice can reform faster on the now-partially-cleared surface → faster blockage than original. The pilot who pulls carb heat OFF when the engine runs rough after application has made a fatal diagnostic error. The initial roughness IS the ice melting — it is the diagnosis confirming that carb heat is correct. Maintain FULL ON until smooth recovery. Option A validates the wrong action. Option C invents a pulse-cycle technique that does not reflect POH or AC 20-113 guidance. Option D falsely claims rain prevents carb ice — rain actually supplies additional moisture that can accelerate carburetor ice formation.
questions.sjt_rationale: This is a hazardous Complacency/Resignation pattern: applying carb heat, seeing the expected response (temporarily worse), and concluding the treatment is wrong. The 'it got worse, remove it' response is deeply instinctive but dangerously incorrect for carb icing. The teaching moment: explain WHY it gets worse before it gets better.

questions.text: In actual IMC on an IFR flight plan, a pilot notices the airspeed indicator is reading approximately 15 knots HIGHER than expected for the power setting and configuration. The aircraft is in level flight. No master caution has illuminated. What should the pilot suspect and what is the SAFEST action?

options.label: A
options.text: The aircraft has encountered an unexpected tailwind aloft — increase power to maintain planned airspeed; log the unexpected tailwind on the pilot weather report (PIREP) for other aircraft in the area

options.label: B
options.text: Pitot tube may be blocked with the drain hole open (ice or obstruction) — a blocked pitot tube with open drain causes the ASI to slowly rise as the trapped air inside the pitot expands with altitude gain or shows erratic readings; alternatively, the pitot heat should be confirmed ON; cross-check the airspeed against power setting, attitude, and VSI; if the ASI diverges from expected values, treat as a pitot failure and fly attitude and power

options.label: C
options.text: The static port has failed and is reading higher than actual — a failed static port always causes the ASI to over-read; selecting the alternate static source will immediately correct the ASI to its true value; no further action is required once alternate static is selected

options.label: D
options.text: A software calibration error has occurred in the ADC (air data computer) — modern glass cockpit avionics occasionally produce ASI spikes during flight; cycle the avionics master switch to reset the ADC; if the reading persists after reset, use the backup ASI if available

questions.explanation: A suspected pitot system anomaly in IMC is a serious instrument failure scenario. The correct response has multiple layers: (1) DIAGNOSE: verify pitot heat is ON (it should always be on in IMC/visible moisture below +5°C). Confirm whether the reading divergence fits a specific failure pattern. A pitot tube blocked with drain hole open causes ASI to slowly drift toward zero (or show erratic low readings), not necessarily high. A pitot + drain both blocked can cause ASI to act like an altimeter (increases with altitude). (2) CROSS-CHECK: compare ASI to: power setting + attitude (if attitude indicator is functioning), rate of climb/descent (if VSI is reliable — which it is in a pitot failure scenario since VSI uses static only), and ATC radar-based groundspeed if in two-way contact. (3) FLY ATTITUDE + POWER: if ASI is unreliable, revert to the fundamental attitude-power relationship (attitude determines pitch and bank; power determines energy state). A 15-knot high reading in level flight at constant power is enough to suspect the pitot system before assuming a tailwind of that magnitude appeared silently. Option A normalizes a 15-knot unexplained speed increase as a tailwind — this complacency pattern in actual IMC is dangerous. Option C incorrectly asserts that static port failure always causes ASI over-reading — the pattern depends on whether pitot or static is blocked.
questions.sjt_rationale: The core skill is Systematic Cross-Check — any single instrument reading that diverges from the integrated picture (power, attitude, other instruments) requires the pilot to suspect the instrument first, not reshape the flight narrative around the instrument. In IMC, unexplained instrument divergence is a red flag that demands immediate systematic analysis, not rationalization.
